title: Someone finally graded the chart tricks retail traders swear by

study.citation: Darmanin, A. (2026), "Retail Trader's Ruin: An Anatomy of Popular Signal Failure", arXiv:2607.20093 [q-fin.ST]

tldr: Five of the most-promoted chart-reading strategies were put through a test whose rules were written in advance, and four of them were ruled out while none of them passed.

sections.body: Spend ten minutes in any trading forum and you will meet the same cast of characters: the golden cross, the RSI, Bollinger Bands, candlestick patterns with names like hammer and engulfing, sell in May and go away. Millions of people trade real money on these rules. The usual way they get defended is a chart with an arrow on it. The usual way they get tested is worse: try a hundred variations, publish the one that looked good, stop. Adam Darmanin asked a plainer question. If you write the passing grade down before you look at the data, does any of it pass?

He took five families of popular signals and set three hurdles in advance. First, does the edge survive the fact that testing many rules guarantees some will look lucky? Second, is what remains still worth anything after trading costs, charged at ten basis points for a round trip, a tenth of one percent, with checks from five up to twenty? Third, would a real trader with a finite account survive the losing stretches under normal margin limits? He ran the rules on decades of daily data for the NASDAQ-100, SPY, and lists of Russell 3000 and S&P 500 members built to include the companies that later vanished.

Nothing passed. Four families were ruled out: the oscillators, on-balance volume, the calendar rule, and the seven-pattern candlestick battery, whose measured effects were so small they sat near zero. The oscillator family came out worse than its benchmark both statistically and after costs. Trend following landed in a third bucket, unresolved, with a range of possible outcomes too wide to call. Crucially, so did the one strategy included because it is known to be real, academic momentum. The test declined to condemn a genuine effect, which is the sign that its verdicts mean something.

Finance has a backtest problem. Comb a price history hard enough and it will confess to anything, which is why so many published market edges shrink or vanish once someone else tries them. What is interesting here is the grading scheme. Instead of the usual pass-fail verdict, every claim lands in one of three buckets: supported, refuted, or unresolved. That third bucket is honest bookkeeping, because failing to find an effect is weak evidence when your sample is small. Building a known-real strategy into the test as a control is the kind of quality check that market research has mostly skipped.

This is a preprint by a single author, posted five days ago and not yet through peer review, so treat the specific verdicts as provisional. The families were judged on different universes and different holding frequencies because the data forced it, which makes them awkward to compare. There was no untouched holdout sample, since these price histories have been picked over for decades. Costs were modeled as a flat charge per trade, with no attempt to capture real spreads and slippage. And refuted means refuted at these thresholds on this data, which is a narrower claim than never works.

terms.def: If you try enough strategies, a few will look brilliant by pure luck, so a fair test has to raise the bar in proportion to how many things you tried.
One hundredth of one percent, the unit traders use for costs; a ten basis point round trip means a tenth of a percent lost getting in and out of a position.
A case you already believe is real, slipped into the experiment to check that your method can still detect something when something is there.

takeaways: A chart rule with a name and a following is not evidence; the evidence is whether it clears a bar someone set before looking.
Costs kill more strategies than markets do, and the more often a rule tells you to trade, the more of its edge it hands to the broker.
When a test says unresolved, believe it. That is different from a green light and different from a debunking, and most headlines flatten it into one of the two.

quiz.q: Why did the study include academic momentum, a strategy already believed to be real?
choices: To give retail traders a strategy they could copy instead
As a control, to check the method could still detect a real effect
Because momentum is the most popular retail signal
To measure how much trading costs have risen since the 1990s
quiz.why: A test that flunks everything is worthless, since you cannot tell a strict test from a broken one. Slipping in a case you believe is genuine checks that the machinery still responds when there is something to find. Momentum landed in the unresolved bucket, which shows the design was not simply condemning every strategy it touched.

quiz.q: What is the multiple-testing problem the study had to correct for?
choices: Trading the same signal on several exchanges at once
Running the same backtest twice and getting different answers
Testing many rules, so a few look profitable by luck alone
Using data from more than one country
quiz.why: Try a hundred coin-flipping rules on the same price history and a handful will show a beautiful record for no reason at all. Corrections raise the bar in proportion to how many rules were tried, so only a genuinely strong strategy clears the bar, and the luckiest member of a big batch gets filtered out.

quiz.q: What did the study conclude about the five popular signal families?
choices: All five worked once trading costs were removed
Four were ruled out and none passed all three hurdles
Candlestick patterns passed while the rest failed
The results were identical across every family tested
quiz.why: Oscillators, on-balance volume, the calendar rule, and the candlestick battery were ruled out on statistical or economic grounds. Trend following was left unresolved, its range of outcomes too wide to call either way. Zero of the tested families cleared all three hurdles, which is a harsher result than any single failure.
